name: Insecure deserialization
description:
The application deserializes a value the client controls - a cookie, a query parameter or a form field - with a deserializer that builds objects of a type the data itself names: Java's ObjectInputStream, PHP's unserialize(), Python's pickle, or a JSON binder with polymorphic typing enabled (Jackson's @class, fastjson's @type). An attacker who controls the bytes chooses which classes are instantiated and in what state, and a chain of ordinary library classes (a "gadget chain") reachable that way commonly turns this into remote code execution, file access or denial of service.

burpsy proves the deserialization without sending a gadget: two values of the same length and encoding, one a deserializer accepts (for example a stream of a nonexistent class, or a resolvable JDK collection class) and one it rejects (the same stream with a corrupted type code, or a nonexistent class name), are answered consistently and differently, which nothing treating the value as an opaque string can do. A finding at low severity and tentative confidence means only that the server builds an object from unsigned JSON in a cookie: a client can forge its fields, but no class choice was shown.

This row is burpsy's own: Burp's catalogue has only the passive 'Serialized object in HTTP message' row, and leaves active deserialization testing to extensions. It is classified under CWE-502.
remediation:
Do not deserialize data the client can modify. Keep state on the server and give the client an opaque identifier, or exchange plain data (JSON bound to one fixed, non-polymorphic type) and validate it like any other input.

Where serialized state must travel through the client, sign it with a server-side key (an HMAC) and verify the signature before the bytes reach any parser. Turn off polymorphic typing in JSON binders (Jackson activateDefaultTyping, fastjson autoType, Json.NET TypeNameHandling) or restrict it to an explicit allowlist, and install a class allowlist on Java object streams (ObjectInputFilter). Never unpickle or unserialize() client data; PHP's allowed_classes option and Python's restricted unpicklers reduce but do not remove the risk.
